title: The Unofficial Choe Show Trailer on Hulu
summary: A two-minute official-channel promotional montage combining multiple voices and music. It begins with a first-person account of addiction, loss of control, self-dislike, childhood trauma, lying, repeated promises to stop, pleasure intertwined with shame and self-directed “perv/monster” labels. A reacting voice describes identification and retrospective acceptance. After music, other fragments move through shared brokenness, emotions in the body, a feelings check, affirmation, an inner-child address to “little David” about fear of being sent away, and an exchange ending “Can you love yourself?” / “I’m gonna try.” Every difficult admission remains uncensored. Addiction is self-identification rather than external diagnosis; private conduct is not inferred; inner-child language is guided dialogue rather than recovered memory or complete biography. Four damaged clauses remain listening-required. Montage cuts and spoken “Dave” do not create publisher-labeled turns; zero named turns ship.

speaker_policy.reason: Music and editing join several voices without caption prefixes. Spoken “Dave/little David” establishes address, not full turn identity. Publish zero named turns and require held-out audiovisual validation before any enrollment.

connections.relationship: The opening speaker cannot simply enjoy the show because it activates fear about their own addictive pattern.
Addiction language is first-person identity, not an archive diagnosis.
Taking things far is linked to loss of control.
Compulsion is rooted by the speaker in a disliked part of self.
“Joke/not an artist” appears as harsh self-talk rather than an external review.
Trauma, behavior, lying and work are combined in the speaker’s causal account.
A vow to stop is followed by reported inability to stop.
Pleasure and shame occur as one intertwined sequence.
The speaker keeps the behavior nonspecific while locating shame around body and privacy.
Severe moralized labels are self-directed and not adopted by the archive.
Caption damage blocks a confident transition into enduring pain.
A montage cut moves from confession to another person’s reaction.
The reacting speaker says the account mirrors their own experience.
Current life is credited to every prior event occurring as it did.
The trailer moves into a different therapeutic/philosophical montage.
A universal metaphor reduces isolation but is not a diagnosis.
Brokenness is reframed as the location of light.
Love, joy and sadness lead into a body-location prompt.
A named emotional-awareness practice precedes affirmation.
The adult/inner-child exercise addresses fear of being sent away.
The adult self reassures the child-self that the old parental context no longer controls the present.
The exercise answers placement fear with present safety.
One participant’s love leads directly to the question of self-love.
The response avoids a false instant cure and commits only to trying.

source_notes: The upload calls itself an unofficial trailer and references Hulu.
The exact compulsive/private behavior is not stated.
The work-related clause near 31 seconds is damaged.
The “earning/learning” phrase near 55 seconds is unresolved.
The clause before the second “little David” is damaged.
The feelings check and inner-child dialogue are practices depicted in the montage, not validated treatment.
Parent/sent-away material is not independently verified biography.
“I love you, Dave” is audible address but not a full diarization label.
The final “I’m gonna try” preserves uncertainty rather than claiming instant healing.
